messages.subject: Imputing missing infection loads in multistate CMR models
messages.subject_clean: Imputing missing infection loads in multistate CMR models
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am currently working on multistate Jolly-Seber models with four states: not yet entered, alive but not infected, alive but infected, and dead. I am interested in the survival probabilities of infected and uninfected individuals and transition probabilities between the infected and uninfected states. In addition to the infection state of captured animals, I also have their infection loads, which I would like to use as a predictor on the survival probability of infected individuals.

Obviously, I am missing infection loads for every occasion that an individual wasn't captured. I would like to follow the method outlined in AHM1 where missing covariate values are imputed from a sub-model, and this has been done at least once before in the literature for our disease system (Spitzen-van der Sluijs et al. 2017).

I would like to ask your opinions on the validity of this method when there are more missing values than there are actual values. For example, many animals were only captured a small proportion of the total number of surveys. If they were infected at least some of the time, and if I were to impute missing values with the mean of the measured infection loads, I would always get non-zero values of infection even if animals weren't infected.

I suppose I'm overall uncertain how JAGS uses these covariate values for occasions when animals weren't captured. Does the model estimate the infection state of individuals on occasions that they weren't captured? If so, will it use the imputed infection load for these occasions to influence parameter estimates?

Hopefully some of my questions are clear enough for some of you to give some input on. Alternatively, if there's another way to incorporate infection load into survival estimates of infected animals I'd love to hear some ideas.

Thanks to everyone for taking the time to read this far.

Kind regards,
Matt Hollanders

The Rhats reported in Marc's example were calculated using coda::gelman.diag, assuming they came from jagsUI.

Ken

messages.body_plain:
Dear unmarked/hmecology readers, my colleague Di Prosser is hiring a post-doc here at Patuxent. Please see info below.
regards
andy

Quantitative Ecologist
Summary:
Dr. Diann Prosser’s Lab of the USGS Patuxent Wildlife Research Center is searching for a highly motivated and talented quantitative researcher or statistician to work on a suite of ecology, spatial modeling, and avian disease research.  This position will consist primarily of quantitative modeling and statistical consulting focusing on animal movement analyses, wildlife disease prevalence and risk modeling, as well as distribution, forecasting and ensemble modeling. There may be opportunities to participate in field work, although this is not a focus of this position. The Patuxent Wildlife Research Center is a world-renowned research institution located within 30 minutes of Annapolis, Baltimore, and Washington, D.C.

Types of services required:  Examples of potential working tasks include designing and/or performing analyses on a variety of datasets including wild bird satellite, GSM, and nanotag telemetry data; creating ensemble models to assess risk of zoonotic disease emergence from wild to domestic populations including avian influenza viruses; waterbird population modeling; and agent based modeling with wildlife disease applications. In addition to the main projects included in this position, the successful applicant will be asked to regularly consult on analytical methods for previously collected data as well as the design of new studies. Co-authorship on publications is encouraged. Proficiency in R is essential, with experience in ArcGIS being beneficial. The candidate must be willing to assist with various projects other than those mentioned above, as this lab works on a variety of topics.

Required expertise/skills:
The ideal candidate has a doctoral degree in Ecology, Wildlife Biology, Statistics, Natural Resources, GIS, Mathematics, or a related field.   Experience with both frequentist and Bayesian methods is required, as is demonstrated proficiency with a wide breadth of analytical methods for ecological analyses. Candidates with Spatial, Movement Ecology, Forecasting, Machine Learning, and High Performance Computing experience is a plus. The candidate must be highly motivated and able to work independently, as well as have strong capacity to communicate well with the team.

Principal Duty Station:  This position will be based at the USGS Patuxent Wildlife Research Center, 12100 Beech Forest Road, Laurel, MD 20705 and is contracted through Natural Systems Analysts, Inc.  Start date is flexible depending on top candidate, however, January 2021 is desired. Given COVID-19 restrictions, some flexibility will be given to remote start date versus on-site. Salary is approximately $59K with benefits. The position is funded for 1 year with potential for 3-4 years depending on performance and fund availability.
How to apply:   Send the following to Dr. Prosser’s Lab at pwrc_app...@usgs.gov with “Quantitative Ecologist” in the Subject header: Cover letter, CV, writing sample, and 3 references in a SINGLE Word or PDF document titled with your name (eg. JohnDoe.doc or JaneSmith.pdf).  Closing date is December 3, 2020; however, applications will be reviewed as received and the position will be filled as soon as a highly qualified candidate is identified.

messages.subject_clean: Do I have a good model if I have to run millions of iterations?
messages.body_plain:
20 million iterations for such a small dataset suggests something is not quite right - either with the model or the data. My first guess in the troubleshooting process would be to examine the way you are defining the survey occasions.

I think Fernando is right that you should be able to fit a null model fairly easily, i.e. constant psi and p. If you can't, there's a good chance the issue is with the data.

messages.subject: Re: Do I have a good model if I have to run millions of iterations?
messages.subject_clean: Do I have a good model if I have to run millions of iterations?
messages.body_plain:
I definitely recommend simulating a test dataset and running it through the model. It's the best way to assess and troubleshoot your model. You can start with a very simple dataset and then start adding wrinkles (covariates, random noise, alternative ecological or observational processes) to test the edges of the model and see where it works and where it fails. This is a great practice to get into and in this case will help you assess whether there are data issues, model issues, or data-model mismatch issues.

Best of luck,
Daniel Hocking

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

our research group at the San Diego Zoo is looking for a Senior Research
Associate to help with the development of data pipelines for our camera
trap studies around the world and to help with our conservation
technology lab. This is an entry-level position with a lot of potential
to learn and grow.

Senior Research Associate – San Diego Zoo Global

The Population Sustainability team is looking for a motivated Senior
Research Associate to support our large-carnivore research programs and
the Conservation Technology Lab. The successful candidate will help with
the processing and management of large camera trap datasets from across
the world, will write scripts and build data pipelines for efficiently
importing and exporting camera trap data in different formats, will
support our Zooniverse sites (AmazonCam Tambopata and Wildwatch Kenya),
and will help with data analysis. The candidate will also support the
Conservation Technology Lab in a variety of tasks from developing data
pipelines for a variety of sensors, to building relational databases,
training machine learning models, developing software for
microcontrollers and single board computers, as well as helping out with
hardware development and testing.

This position requires strong quantitative skills as well as proficiency
in R and Python programming. A background in geographic information
systems (GIS), C/C++ programming, relational databases, as well as
occupancy and capture-recapture models are a plus. The position will be
based at the Institute for Conservation Research in Escondido, CA.
Experience and proficiency with Linux, Bash scripting, NumPy, SciPy,
pandas, OpenCV and Git will be considered an asset.

More details can be found here:

https://us59.dayforcehcm.com/CandidatePortal/en-US/sdzg/Posting/View/2317

Thanks,

Mathias
